fact_text: A third-country national relocating to Greece for employment must obtain a national (type D) long-stay visa from a Greek consulate before entering the country; the Ministry of Foreign Affairs publishes the general supporting documents and procedure for granting these National D-type visas. A short-stay Schengen (type C) or visa-free entry does not permit taking up work.
evidence_quote: General Supporting Documents & Procedure for Granting National D- type visas

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a professional can start work during 90-day visa-free or Schengen (type C) entry. Actually employment requires a national (type D) long-stay visa issued by a Greek consulate before arrival. Action: apply for the type-D national visa at the consulate before travelling.

fact_text: After entering on a type-D visa, a third-country professional must hold a residence permit for dependent employment (Article 15) to live and work in Greece. The Ministry of Migration and Asylum lists it under the 'Residence Permit for Employment and Professional Reasons' category, each with its own required supporting documents.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the entry visa is enough to work in Greece. Actually the visa only authorises entry; a separate residence permit for dependent employment (Article 15) is required to live and work. Action: apply for the Article-15 residence permit after arrival.

fact_text: The dependent-employment route is employer-initiated: the Greek employer must file an application for approval of 'metaklisi' (recruitment of a worker from abroad) before the third-country national can obtain the entry visa and residence permit. The worker cannot begin the process on their own.
evidence_quote: Αίτηση εργοδότη για την έγκριση μετάκλησης

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the worker applies for their own Greek work permit. Actually the employer must first obtain approval of the 'metaklisi' (recruitment from abroad). Action: have the Greek employer file and win the metaklisi approval before any visa step.

fact_text: Highly-skilled third-country professionals can apply for the EU Blue Card, which the Ministry lists under a distinct 'highly-skilled employment (Blue Card)' category, separate from the ordinary dependent-employment permit. It carries its own eligibility conditions (a qualifying skilled job offer and salary level) and EU mobility rights.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed all foreign hires use the same work permit. Actually highly-skilled hires can use the EU Blue Card, a separate residence-permit category with a salary threshold and intra-EU mobility. Action: check whether the role and salary qualify for the Blue Card before defaulting to the Article-15 permit.

fact_text: A Greek residence permit is granted for a specific purpose and employment relationship. Moving between purposes (for example from dependent employment to independent financial activity) is treated as a change in residence status that requires a corresponding change or renewal of the permit, not a free switch.
evidence_quote: Renewal for dependent employment purposes, provision of services and work or independent financial activity due to a change in residence status

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed a residence permit lets you take any job or go self-employed. Actually the permit is purpose-bound; changing employment purpose requires changing the residence-permit status. Action: apply to change the permit before switching employer type or purpose.

fact_text: A third-country professional who is present in Greece for more than 183 days cumulatively within any twelve-month period becomes a Greek tax resident from the first day of presence, and is then taxed in Greece on worldwide income under the Income Tax Code (Law 4172/2013).
evidence_quote: An individual being in Greece for a period exceeding one hundred eighty-three (183) days, cumulatively, during any twelve-month period, shall be considered a Greek tax resident

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you are only taxed in Greece after a full calendar year or once you formally 'settle'. Actually crossing 183 days in any 12-month window makes you a Greek tax resident from day one, taxable on worldwide income. Action: track days in Greece and plan tax residency before the 183-day line.

fact_text: A third-country national needs a Greek Tax Identification Number (AFM/TIN) to be employed, paid and taxed in Greece. AADE can issue the TIN together with a TAXISnet Authentication Key to a person still resident abroad, and a legal or tax representative may apply on their behalf, so the AFM can be arranged before arrival.
evidence_quote: Issuance of Tax Identification Number and Authentication Key at the same time to tax residents abroad

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you can only get a Greek AFM in person after arriving. Actually AADE issues the TIN and Authentication Key to persons abroad, and a tax representative can apply for you. Action: obtain the AFM via a representative before you relocate so payroll can start on arrival.

entity_title: Article 5C special taxation for new tax residents
fact_text: A professional who transfers their tax residence to Greece and earns salaried employment income here may qualify for the Article 5C special method of taxation of income from employment or business activity, an incentive the State offers to attract new tax residents. It is applied for through AADE and is distinct from ordinary income taxation.
evidence_quote: Article 5C – Special method of taxation of income from employment or business activity

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed relocating professionals are simply taxed at standard Greek rates. Actually a new tax resident who takes up Greek employment can apply for the Article 5C special taxation regime. Action: check Article 5C eligibility and its deadline with AADE before your first Greek tax filing.

entity_title: AMKA (Social Insurance Number) and e-EFKA registration
fact_text: To be hired, insured and paid in Greece a third-country worker must have an AMKA (Social Insurance Number) and be registered as an insuree of e-EFKA, the Electronic National Social Insurance Institution. The residence or work permit alone does not create the social-insurance registration.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the residence/work permit is enough to be put on payroll. Actually you separately need an AMKA (Social Insurance Number) and e-EFKA registration before an employer can insure and pay you. Action: obtain the AMKA and register with e-EFKA at the very start of employment.

fact_text: Greece has bilateral social-security conventions with a number of specific third countries (per e-EFKA these include Egypt, the USA, Canada, Australia, Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay, Venezuela, Serbia, Syria, Moldova, New Zealand and Libya). A worker from such a country may aggregate insurance and pension periods between the two systems.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed contributions paid abroad are lost when you move to Greece. Actually if your home country has a bilateral social-security convention with Greece, insurance/pension periods can be aggregated. Action: check whether your home country is on e-EFKA's bilateral-convention list.
